node.label: Carolyn Strange
node.date_label: Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) · Making Good, with Tina Loo (1997) · Honour, Violence and Emotions in History, coedited (2014) · Discretionary Justice (2016)
node.description: In Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995), Carolyn Strange argues that Toronto projected its anxieties about urban industrialization onto young wage-earning women, making their work and leisure targets of moral regulation. She shows social agencies and the city’s Morality Department meeting young working women with a mixture of paternalism and suspicion. With Tina Loo, Making Good (1997) follows law and moral regulation as contested processes of defining Canadian citizenship. Rebecca Murdock praised the first book’s research and recovery of working women’s history but questioned its periodization and wanted more explicit feminist and class analysis. Cynthia Comacchio later asked whether its account of sexual geography, considered alongside Karen Dubinsky’s work, sufficiently included sexual expression within the home. Joan Sangster credited Strange’s reinterpretation of the Bell Telephone strike’s medical testimony with explaining medical knowledge as social power. Strange’s later work includes the jointly edited Honour, Violence and Emotions in History (2014) and Discretionary Justice (2016), which treats pardon and parole as enduring, related forms of discretionary power.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Toronto’s Girl Problem: The Perils and Pleasures of the City, 1880–1930 (1995); Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada, 1867–1939 (1997), with Tina Loo; Honour, Violence and Emotions in History (2014), coedited with Robert Cribb and Christopher E. Forth; Discretionary Justice: Pardon and Parole in New York from the Revolution to the Depression (2016).

proposed_edges.relationship: The ANU synopsis of Strange’s 2024 remembrance identifies Davis’s Fiction in the Archives (originally 1987) as a major influence on Strange’s career.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: ANU event notice, 27 March 2024, Strange abstract, first paragraph: “the greater impact on Strange’s career.” This is the seminar synopsis, not a reading of the lecture. The notice gives 1990 without identifying an edition; 1987 is retained from existing source nzd_fiction_1987. No new interpretation of Davis’s book is asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Fiction in the Archives as a career influence

proposed_edges.relationship: Sangster’s 2011 introduction identifies Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) as a conscious use of Foucault to study the discourses regulating women.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sangster, Through Feminist Eyes (2011), introduction, printed 26 (PDF page 34), with note 104 at 46 (PDF page 54): “drew consciously on Foucault.” Named-reader attribution; Toronto’s introduction was available only as a short JSTOR opening. No particular Foucault text or sole intellectual origin established.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Discovering Women’s History” (2011), Sangster credits Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) with reinterpreting the medical testimony she had used for the 1907 Bell Telephone strike.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sangster, printed 50 (PDF page 58), paragraph beginning At the time; note 3 at 52 identifies the 1995 book. She credits “new analytical tools” for explaining medical knowledge as social power. This is Sangster’s 2011 retrospective recognition, not a claim that Strange influenced Sangster’s earlier strike article. Original monograph unread in full.
proposed_edges.map_label: Sangster credits a revised reading of medical testimony

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio asks whether the spatial account in Strange’s Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995), discussed alongside Dubinsky, gives sufficient attention to sexual expression within the parental home.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Comacchio, printed 193–194 (PDF pages 27–28), paragraph beginning Engaging this concept and its continuation before The Second Greatest Disappointment: “truly limited to public spaces.” A qualified question about both books, not rejection of Strange’s argument. Her text’s 1993 date for Strange is corrected using the publisher’s 1995 metadata; full essay and books unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions the emphasis on public sexual spaces

proposed_edges.relationship: Making Good (1997), coauthored with Tina Loo, explains law and moral regulation as a struggle over Canadian citizenship, in Tom Mitchell’s review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mitchell, Making Good discussion, opening three substantive paragraphs: “site of struggle.” Read as a named reviewer’s account; original book unread. Existing moral_regulation roster already lists Strange and is preserved. Existing field links edge_858, edge_862 and edge_964 do not supply this person’s endpoint relationship.

proposed_edges.relationship: Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) shows young wage-earning women in Toronto becoming a focus of anxieties about industrialization and female sexuality, whom social agencies sought to protect and the city's Morality Department sought to control, a mixture of paternalism and suspicion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Rebased on Rebecca Murdock’s complete CBRA review, review opening paragraph, and Joan Sangster, Through Feminist Eyes (2011), introduction, paragraph beginning “Carolyn Strange’s positioning” and note 104. Murdock supports the industrialization, sexuality, social-agency and Morality Department claims; Sangster locates the book’s analysis of regulation in Canadian feminist historiography. Earlier publisher and book references remain bibliographic context; neither is claimed as freshly read in full.
proposed_edges.map_label: Working women and the urban girl problem

proposed_edges.relationship: Honour, Violence and Emotions in History (2014), coedited with Robert Cribb and Christopher E. Forth, brings historically specific emotions into the comparative study of honour and violence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Bloomsbury publisher description, first two paragraphs, editor byline and contents chapter 1/afterword; phrases “historically specific understandings” and “history of honour and violence.” Publisher-level statement of the collection’s program, with all editors credited. Chapters unread; this does not establish Strange’s adoption of any particular theorist of emotion.
proposed_edges.map_label: Honour, violence and historically specific feeling

proposed_edges.relationship: In Manly Militants, Cohesive Communities, and Defiant Domestics (1995), Franca Iacovetta praises Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) for integrating class, race and gender in its analysis of urban wage-earning women, presenting it as an example in her argument for more integrative historical scholarship.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected journal PDF text read, especially pp. 248–251. This is an evaluative literature survey, not a standalone book review or a stated intellectual debt. The body explicitly assesses Strange’s analytical method; the edge records positive reception as an undirected comparison.
proposed_edges.map_label: Commends integrated class, race and gender analysis

proposed_edges.relationship: Toronto’s Girl Problem (1995) contributes a feminist perspective to urban history by relating young women’s work, leisure and public presence to Toronto’s industrial transformation and the discourses that treated working women as a moral problem, as its 1996 Urban History review explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher’s first-page image visually read. Only p. 270 was available; the continuation, signature and original book remain unread. Reviewer authorship is left unresolved because the landing-page byline combines multiple names. The field assessment is explicit on the page.
proposed_edges.map_label: Feminist interpretation of the industrial city

proposed_edges.relationship: Stories of Their Lives: The Historian and the Capital Case File (1998) contributes to interpreting archives as constructed records of power by examining how officials turned competing voices into authoritative case narratives, an approach Alison Frank Johnson and Robert Nemes apply in Beyond the Verdict (2025).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected publisher article passages and notes 40, 82 and 91 read; original chapter unread. Field mapping is editorial, limited to document construction and official authority. Both later authors lack eligible person endpoints, so no person edges are proposed. The article first appeared online in 2025; its volume is dated 2026.
proposed_edges.map_label: Capital case files as constructions of authority
